title: Short Stuff: Frances Kelsey: Hero of the FDA
summary: A Short Stuff episode honoring Frances Kelsey, the FDA medical reviewer who refused to approve the sedative thalidomide (called philidamide in the transcript) in 1960 over insufficient safety data, keeping it off the U.S. market while it caused birth defects in Europe. The hosts cover the drug's history and marketing, the German and Australian doctors who linked it to limb deformities, the mechanism behind the defects, Kelsey's 1962 recognition (including the Washington Post article and the Kefauver-Harris Amendment), and her long FDA career.
topics: President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service

segments.title: Introduction and Kelsey's reputation
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as a tribute to Frances Kelsey, a lesser-known 20th-century hero, and note that she received recognition in her lifetime, including an FDA award named for her.

segments.title: Kelsey's background and joining the FDA
segments.summary: Kelsey was born Frances Oldham on Vancouver Island, earned degrees in Montreal and a PhD in pharmacology from the University of Chicago, married Fremont Kelsey, and joined the FDA in Washington, D.C. in the early 1960s, when drug review was less rigorous and reviewers had about sixty days.

segments.title: Thalidomide application arrives at the FDA
segments.summary: About seven months after she started, Kelsey received a new drug application for the sedative philidamide (thalidomide) from Richardson Merrill, a drug that had been widely used in Europe and elsewhere.

segments.title: Thalidomide as a sedative and its uses
segments.summary: The hosts describe philidamide as a post-war sedative and anti-anxiety drug from the 1950s, popular in West Germany and elsewhere, and used by pregnant women for morning sickness. The company pushed for quick approval.

segments.title: Kelsey's refusal and the company's pressure
segments.summary: Kelsey found reports of neuropathy and no studies on pregnant women, so she demanded more data. The company returned six times. Kelsey suspected drugs could cross the placenta, contrary to the thinking of the time. Hosts note German testing focused only on toxicity.

segments.title: Birth defects in Europe
segments.summary: Doctors William McBride in Australia and Widukind Lenz in Germany noticed clusters of children born with limb deformities and linked them to early-pregnancy use of the drug, which was sold over the counter in West Germany. About ten thousand children were affected and roughly forty percent died around birth.

segments.title: U.S. cases and the drug's mechanism
segments.summary: Kelsey kept the drug off the U.S. market, though fewer than about twenty American children were born with defects, possibly from drug obtained while traveling. The hosts explain that the drug binds non-selectively to proteins that control gene expression, which was only understood about sixty years later.

segments.title: Recognition and the Kefauver-Harris Amendment
segments.summary: A 1962 Washington Post article brought Kelsey attention and led to a presidential civilian service award. The Kefauver-Harris Amendment then tightened and lengthened the FDA approval process.

segments.title: Kelsey's later career
segments.summary: Kelsey stayed at the FDA for about forty-five more years and helped shape its drug approval process. The hosts joke about the current approval process.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and the show credits iHeartRadio and podcast platforms.
